title: What a communication plan does for a project
blurb: Explain the benefits a communication plan brings to a project, and what goes wrong when communication is left to chance.
question: A GP practice is introducing online appointment booking. The practice manager says a communication plan is 'just paperwork' and that people will hear about it anyway. What benefits would a communication plan bring to this project?

teach.h: Communication on purpose, not by accident
teach.body: A communication plan sets out, in advance, who will be told what, when, how and by whom, and how feedback will come back. Its benefits to a project are that messages are consistent, timely and targeted; expectations are managed; support is built; misunderstanding and rumour are reduced; effort is used efficiently; responsibilities are clear; and engagement and adoption of the change are supported. In plain English: people hear the right thing, at the right time, from the right person.

teach.body: A project can hit its time, cost and quality targets and still be judged a failure if stakeholders expected something else. Planned communication manages those expectations by being honest about progress, constraints and changes early. It also builds the support a project needs to clear obstacles, and it prepares users for the change so they actually adopt the outputs. Without adoption, the benefits in the business case are never realised.

With no plan, reception staff hear a rumour that online booking will cut their jobs, older patients find the phone line suddenly shorter, and two GPs give patients different launch dates. With a plan: the practice manager briefs reception first, face to face, explaining their new role; GPs work from one set of key messages; patients get texts, posters and a helpline number four weeks ahead; and feedback from the first fortnight is reviewed and acted on.

teach.caption: In both, the plan makes communication deliberate rather than reactive.

teach.text: A communication plan does NOT guarantee that stakeholders will agree, remove all conflict, or replace stakeholder engagement. And more communication is not automatically better: copying everyone into everything causes information overload. The benefit comes from targeted, planned messages.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name a benefit clearly, e.g. 'consistent messages from a single agreed source'.
Explain how the plan creates it, e.g. agreed key messages and a named sender for each.
Link it to project success, e.g. fewer misunderstandings, so less rework and conflict.
Use a different benefit for each bullet the question asks for; don't repeat one idea.
Where helpful, contrast with what happens without a plan: rumour, surprises, resistance.
Benefits: consistent, timely, targeted messages and managed expectations.
Builds support and reduces misunderstanding and rumour.
Efficient: effort goes on messages people need, with clear responsibilities.
Supports engagement and adoption of the change, which leads to benefits.
It does not guarantee agreement, and more messages is not the same as better communication.

summary: You can now explain the benefits a communication plan brings to a project, and link each one to project success. You can also spot the common distractors, such as claims that a plan guarantees agreement or that sending everyone everything is a benefit.

A.q: Which of the following is a benefit to a project of having a communication plan?
options: It removes the need for a risk register
It keeps messages consistent and timely
It fixes the project budget in advance
A.why: A plan agrees key messages, senders and timing in advance, so stakeholders get consistent information when they need it.

whyNot.0: Risks still need a risk register; the communication plan doesn't replace it.
whyNot.2: Good communication improves understanding and support, but it can't guarantee agreement.
whyNot.3: The budget is set through cost planning, not by the communication plan.

A.q: How does a communication plan help to reduce rumour on a change project?
options: By restricting information to the board
By sending every single document to everyone
By filling gaps with planned, timely news
A.why: Rumour fills silence. Planned, timely updates give people accurate information before speculation takes hold.

whyNot.0: Restricting information creates the silence in which rumours spread.
whyNot.1: Informal conversation can't be banned, and it is often useful; the fix is accurate planned news.
whyNot.2: Sending everything to everyone causes overload, so important points are missed.

A.q: A communication plan names who is responsible for issuing each message. What is the main benefit of this?
options: Clear accountability, so nothing is missed
Fewer stakeholders need to be identified
The sponsor no longer needs to be involved
Messages no longer need to be tailored
A.why: Named responsibility means each message has an owner, so communications aren't forgotten or duplicated.

whyNot.1: Assigning senders doesn't change how many stakeholders there are.
whyNot.2: The sponsor still has a key communication role, often fronting important messages.
whyNot.3: Tailoring is still needed; ownership is about who sends it, not what it says.

B.q: A project delivers on time and within budget, yet the client is unhappy because they had expected extra features. Which benefit of a communication plan was most clearly missing?
B.why: Unmanaged expectations cause dissatisfaction even when targets are met. Planned, honest communication about scope would have prevented the surprise.

whyNot.0: Reporting cost has nothing to do with the client's mistaken expectations.
whyNot.1: Procurement speed is unrelated to what the client expected to receive.
whyNot.3: A record of decisions helps later, but the core failure was expectations never being set and checked.

B.q: Why does a communication plan make project communication more EFFICIENT?
options: Effort goes on messages people need
Every stakeholder gets the same report
It removes the need for any meetings
The PM sends every message personally
B.why: Because messages are targeted using stakeholder analysis, time isn't wasted producing or reading irrelevant material.

whyNot.1: One report for all is untargeted, which wastes effort for both sender and readers.
whyNot.2: Meetings remain essential for interactive communication; the plan schedules them sensibly.
whyNot.3: The plan spreads responsibility to the right senders rather than funnelling everything through the PM.

B.q: Which is NOT a benefit of a communication plan?
B.why: Communication can reduce misunderstanding-based conflict, but no plan can eliminate conflict altogether.

whyNot.0: Targeting messages to each audience is a core benefit.
whyNot.1: Building support for the project and the change is a key benefit.
whyNot.2: Clear responsibility for preparing and issuing each message is a benefit.

C.q:
Which TWO are benefits of a communication plan?
1. Greater adoption of the change by users
2. A guarantee that the project finishes early
3. Fewer misunderstandings among stakeholders
4. No further need to update stakeholder analysis
C.why: A plan supports adoption of the change and reduces misunderstanding. It guarantees nothing about schedule, and analysis still needs updating.

whyNot.0: No communication plan can guarantee an early finish.
whyNot.2: Neither is a benefit: there is no schedule guarantee, and the analysis must be kept current.
whyNot.3: Stakeholder analysis still needs updating as stakeholders change.

C.q: A retailer is moving all its stores onto a new till system. Store managers learn the go-live date from a supplier's engineer before the project tells them. What does this most suggest?
options: The till system's design is faulty
Store managers have too much power
There is no planned, timely messaging
The go-live date should now be postponed
C.why: Key stakeholders hearing important news second-hand shows communication isn't planned: the right message isn't reaching the right people first.

whyNot.0: Nothing in the scenario suggests a design fault; the failure is in communication.
whyNot.1: Power isn't the issue; the managers simply weren't told in time.
whyNot.3: The date may be fine; what's missing is planned communication about it.

C.q: On an agile project, business users are often asked to attend reviews at short notice and many cannot make it. How would a communication plan most help?
options: By replacing reviews with written reports
By making attendance at reviews optional
By sending the backlog to users each day
By scheduling the review cadence ahead
C.why: Planning the rhythm of reviews in advance lets users book the time, so the frequent feedback an iterative project relies on actually happens.

whyNot.0: Written reports remove the interactive feedback that reviews exist to provide.
whyNot.1: Optional attendance would make the feedback gap worse.
whyNot.2: A daily backlog email adds overload and doesn't solve the attendance problem.

reteach.title: The builder who tells the neighbours
reteach.question: Two builders each put an extension on a terraced house. One plans how to keep the neighbours informed; the other just turns up. Which job runs more smoothly, and why?

blocks.body: The first builder drops a letter through each neighbour's door a fortnight ahead: what's happening, which days will be noisy, when the skip arrives, and one phone number to call. The second just starts. His neighbours hear drilling at 7am, find a skip blocking their drive, and complain to the council. The work is identical. The difference is planned, timely, targeted communication with a named contact.

blocks.text: The planned builder doesn't post a daily diary to every house on the street. Benefits come from the RIGHT information to the RIGHT people, not from sending more of it.

explain.body: A plan agrees the key messages, who sends them and when. That keeps the story consistent across the team, gets news to people before it affects them, and makes sure each group receives what is relevant to them rather than everything or nothing.

items.label: agreed version of the key messages
group gets what is relevant to it

test.q: Two project team members give a supplier different go-live dates. Which benefit of a communication plan would have prevented this?
test.why: Agreed key messages and named senders keep everyone telling the same story.

whyNot.0: Cost of reporting doesn't explain conflicting dates.
whyNot.1: Stakeholder power is not something a plan increases, and it isn't the issue here.
whyNot.3: Procurement speed doesn't stop the team giving contradictory information.

explain.body: Stakeholders judge a project against what they expected. Planned, honest updates on progress, constraints and changes keep those expectations realistic. Regular, relevant contact also builds support: supporters help unblock decisions, release resources and champion the change to others.

test.q: Why does building stakeholder support through planned communication matter to project success?
test.why: Supportive stakeholders help remove blockers, make timely decisions and champion the change.

whyNot.1: Supporters still need communication, or their support can fade.
whyNot.2: The business case justifies the project; support doesn't replace it.
whyNot.3: Support can help manage risks, but it doesn't make them vanish.

explain.body: When people expect news and don't get it, they fill the gap with guesses, and guesses spread. Planned updates close those gaps. Targeting also makes communication efficient: nobody wastes time producing reports no one reads, and readers aren't buried in material that isn't for them.

explain.caption: A plan avoids both extremes: not too little, not too much.

test.q: Staff on a restructuring project start sharing rumours about job losses. What is the most likely communication cause?
test.why: Rumour grows where people expect information and don't receive it; a plan fills that gap with accurate, timely news.

whyNot.0: Face-to-face briefings usually reduce rumour, because people can ask questions.
whyNot.1: A risk register is a management tool and doesn't cause rumours.
whyNot.2: Schedule length isn't a communication cause of rumour.

explain.body: The plan names who prepares and sends each communication, so nothing falls through the gaps. It also prepares users for the change: what it means for them, when, and where to get help. That supports engagement and adoption, and outputs that are actually used are what let benefits be realised.

test.q: A new HR system goes live, but staff keep using their old spreadsheets. Which benefit of a communication plan would most help here?
options: Clearer budget reporting to the board
test.why: Planned communication prepares users, explains what's in it for them and where to get help, which supports adoption.

whyNot.0: Budget reporting to the board doesn't change how staff work.
whyNot.2: Procurement is finished; the issue is users adopting the change.
whyNot.3: Reducing the number of stakeholders mapped doesn't address the users' behaviour.
